title: Controlling Forgetting with Test-Time Data in Continual Learning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to introduce a new continual-learning (CL) setting where unlabeled test-time data is leveraged self-supervised to refresh a model's memory of prior tasks and reduce catastrophic forgetting, particularly in the challenging class-incremental CL (CIL-CL) scenario without a replay buffer. Paper [1] discusses leveraging external unlabeled data to mitigate catastrophic forgetting in CIL, but it relies on queried external data rather than test-time data. Paper [2] uses pseudo-labeling for CIL with additional unlabeled data, but it does not explicitly address self-supervised adaptation during test-time or the absence of a replay buffer. Paper [3] focuses on unsupervised continual learning but does not address leveraging test-time data for memory refresh in CIL-CL. No prior paper explicitly introduces the same purpose of leveraging test-time data self-supervised for memory refresh in CIL-CL without a replay buffer.

### Mechanism
The contribution formalizes a setting where supervised training sessions are interleaved with online unsupervised adaptation on test-time data (processed once and discarded for privacy), drawn from the mixture of all previously seen task distributions, and evaluates on held-out data distinct from the adaptation data. Paper [17] discusses continual test-time domain adaptation (CTTA), where a pre-trained model adapts to continually changing unsupervised target domains, but it does not address interleaving supervised training with unsupervised test-time adaptation or the specific mixture of prior task distributions. Paper [26] also addresses CTTA but focuses on suppressing domain shifts rather than leveraging test-time data for memory refresh in CIL-CL. No prior paper formalizes the same mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its setting on CLIP ViT-B/16 across five vision datasets (Aircraft, CUB, Stanford Cars, Oxford Pets, CIFAR100, plus OOD GTSRB), each split into 10 disjoint-class tasks, using metrics Average Accuracy and Average Forgetting. Paper [4] evaluates rehearsal-free continual learning using Average Accuracy and Average Forgetting, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [24] uses similar metrics for replay-based continual learning in semantic segmentation, which also matches the evaluation design. Although the specific datasets differ, the evaluation design (metrics and continual learning setup) is covered by prior work.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of continual learning with vision-language foundation models. Paper [4] addresses rehearsal-free continual learning in vision tasks, and Paper [24] addresses replay-based continual learning in semantic segmentation, both of which fall within the general domain of continual learning in vision. While the contribution applies to vision-language foundation models, this is a specific instance within the broader domain of continual learning in vision, which is covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to provide a replay-buffer-free method that exploits test-time data to control forgetting while adapting to new tasks. Paper [17] ("Continual Reinforcement Learning Without Replay Buffers") introduces a replay-buffer-free approach for continual reinforcement learning, aiming to avoid catastrophic forgetting while adapting to non-stationary environments. Although the domain differs (reinforcement learning vs continual learning with CLIP), the purpose at the problem-class level — controlling forgetting without replay buffers — is substantively equivalent. 

### Mechanism
The mechanism, DoSAPP, involves gradient-scored sparse updates restricted to the first MLP layer of each transformer block, dual EMA smoothing with distinct momentum for masked/frozen vs selected teacher parameters, and pseudo-labeling based on max-logit confidence. Paper [13] ("Gradient Sparsification For Masked Fine-Tuning of Transformers") uses gradient sparsification for masked fine-tuning, which is equivalent to the sparse updates restricted to specific layers. Paper [31] ("Local Clustering with Mean Teacher for Semi-supervised learning") employs exponential moving average (EMA) smoothing for teacher-student models, which matches the dual EMA smoothing aspect. Paper [27] ("Meta Pseudo Labels") uses pseudo-labeling with teacher-student frameworks, which aligns with the pseudo-labeling mechanism here. Together, these papers cover the mechanism's components.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves continual learning benchmarks (CIL datasets), ablation studies, and comparison against methods with and without experience replay. Paper [4] ("Practical Recommendations for Replay-based Continual Learning Methods") uses continual learning benchmarks and ablation studies to validate replay-based methods, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [23] ("RDumb: A simple approach that questions our progress in continual test-time adaptation") introduces the CCC benchmark for continual test-time adaptation, which aligns with the continual learning evaluation framework. Paper [18] ("Controllable Continual Test-Time Adaptation") also evaluates continual test-time adaptation methods using benchmarks and ablation studies. These papers collectively cover the evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is continual learning/test-time adaptation of CLIP. Paper [3] ("Continual Learning in Open-vocabulary Classification with Complementary Memory Systems") addresses continual learning in open-vocabulary classification using CLIP, which matches the application area. Paper [20] ("Online Zero-Shot Classification with CLIP") studies online zero-shot classification with CLIP, which also falls within the same domain. Paper [18] ("Controllable Continual Test-Time Adaptation") addresses continual test-time adaptation, which overlaps with the domain here. These papers cover the domain.

## PURPOSE: "Provide a concrete, replay-buffer-free method that exploits test-time data to control forgetting while adapting to new tasks."

Paper [17] "Continual Reinforcement Learning Without Replay Buffers" explicitly addresses "continual reinforcement learning... without experience replay (ER) from a large buffer" while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. Paper [19] "Continual Test-Time Domain Adaptation" addresses adapting to continually changing target domains without source data, controlling forgetting. Paper [23] "RDumb" addresses continual test-time adaptation. Paper [18] "Controllable Continual Test-Time Adaptation" addresses CTTA with forgetting control. However, the specific combination of "replay-buffer-free" + "test-time data exploitation" + "forgetting control" in a class-incremental learning (not domain adaptation) setting is closest to [17] at the problem-class level — both aim to eliminate replay buffers while preventing forgetting during continual adaptation. Paper [19] and [18] also cover this purpose in CTTA. The purpose is COVERED by [17], [19], [18].

## MECHANISM: DoSAPP — student-teacher framework with (a) gradient-scored sparse updates restricted to first MLP layer (top-K, c=0.1), (b) dual EMA smoothing with distinct momentum for masked/frozen vs selected teacher params via affine projection of binary mask, (c) unsupervised phase using max-logit OOD-inspired pseudo-label selection between teacher/student, (d) union of prior-task masks.

Breaking this down:
- **Gradient-scored sparse updates (top-K)**: Paper [24] "Training Neural Networks with Fixed Sparse Masks" uses top-K gradient magnitude to construct sparse masks. Paper [13] "Gradient Sparsification For Masked Fine-Tuning" uses gradient sparsification for masked fine-tuning of transformers. Paper [12] "Composable Sparse Fine-Tuning" uses sparse fine-tuning with mask composition (union of masks across tasks is directly described).
- **Student-teacher with EMA**: Paper [19] uses student-teacher with EMA (stochastic restore). Paper [31] "Local Clustering with Mean Teacher" uses EMA-based mean teacher.
- **Dual EMA with distinct momentum for different parameter groups**: This specific "affine projection of binary mask" with two distinct EMA momenta for masked vs. frozen parameters is not clearly described in any prior paper. Paper [19] uses a single EMA. No paper describes dual-momentum EMA via affine projection of a binary mask.
- **Max-logit pseudo-label selection between teacher/student**: Paper [20] "Online Zero-Shot Classification with CLIP" uses confidence-based pseudo-label selection online. Paper [15] discusses noisy student self-training. The specific "take the more confident of teacher vs student" is not explicitly described.
- **Union of prior-task masks**: Paper [12] explicitly describes composing sparse masks via union across tasks.

The combination of dual-EMA via affine projection of binary mask is the most distinctive primitive. No single prior paper covers this specific mechanism. The closest are [24], [13], [12] for sparse masking, and [19], [31] for EMA teacher, but the dual-momentum affine projection is not present. However, the question is whether the UNDERLYING PRIMITIVE is covered. The affine projection of a binary mask to implement dual EMA is essentially: EMA_teacher = m*EMA_teacher + (1-m)*student for selected params, different m for frozen params. This is a parameterized EMA — no prior paper explicitly covers this combination. MECHANISM appears NONE.

## EVALUATION: State-of-the-art comparison on 5 CIL datasets, with/without ER buffer (200), ablation of momentum choices, CLIP ViT-B/16, mean of 5 runs.

Paper [19] evaluates CTTA methods on benchmark datasets with/without replay. Paper [23] evaluates CTTA on benchmarks. Paper [4] "Practical Recommendations for Replay-based Continual Learning Methods" explicitly compares methods with/without replay buffers on CIL benchmarks. The evaluation design (benchmark comparison on CIL datasets, with/without ER, ablation studies) is a standard CIL evaluation design used in [4], [3], [19]. The "with/without ER" comparison design is directly in [4]. EVALUATION is COVERED by [4].

## DOMAIN: Continual learning / test-time adaptation of CLIP

Paper [19] covers continual test-time adaptation. Paper [3] covers continual learning with CLIP. Paper [20] covers online zero-shot classification with CLIP. Paper [18] covers controllable CTTA. The domain of continual learning with CLIP / test-time adaptation is covered by [3], [19], [20].
